snippet.title: The Book Shackleton Ignored
snippet.description:
In 1901, Swedish geologist Otto Nordenskjöld sailed twenty-nine men into the Weddell Sea aboard the Antarctic. The ice crushed his wooden ship over thirty-three days, scattered his expedition across three shelters separated by hundreds of miles, and killed only one man before all twenty-eight survivors converged at the same hut on the same day. Twelve years later, Ernest Shackleton sailed the Endurance into the same sea with a copy of Nordenskjöld's account on his bookshelf. The ice did exactly what the book said it would do.
This documentary covers the 1901-1903 Swedish Antarctic Expedition, Captain Carl Anton Larsen's fourteen-day trek across the Weddell Sea pack after the Antarctic sank, the stone hut on Paulet Island where twenty men wintered on penguin blubber and buried twenty-two-year-old sailor Ole Wennersgaard, and the waist-high shelter at Hope Bay where three men read condensed milk labels for entertainment through ten months of isolation. The Argentine Navy corvette ARA Uruguay, sent south by a country that had contributed one twenty-one-year-old sub-lieutenant to the expedition, brought them all home on December 2nd, 1903. The book Nordenskjöld wrote about it sold poorly. Shackleton packed it for the Endurance anyway.
📚 FURTHER READING

Antarctica, or Two Years Amongst the Ice of the South Pole by Otto Nordenskjöld, J. Gunnar Andersson, Carl A. Larsen, and C. Skottsberg (1905)

#antarctica #exploration #history #survival
The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901 to 1903 is one of the most remarkable survival stories in polar history and one of the least remembered. Otto Nordenskjöld's ship Antarctic was crushed in the Weddell Sea in February 1903, scattering his crew across Snow Hill Island, Paulet Island, and Hope Bay for nearly a year. Captain Carl Anton Larsen later founded the whaling station at Grytviken on South Georgia and built the Lutheran church where Ernest Shackleton's funeral was held in 1922. Nordenskjöld published a meticulous account of how Weddell Sea ice destroys wooden ships. Shackleton carried a copy into the same waters twelve years later. The Endurance sank on October 27th, 1915.

snippet.title: Champlain's colony died of scurvy with the cure on his bookshelf
snippet.description:
Samuel de Champlain lost thirty-five men to scurvy at Saint Croix Island in 1604, sixty-eight years after Domagaya taught Jacques Cartier the cure at Stadacona.

Pierre Dugua de Mons financed the 1604 voyage under Henri IV. Marc Lescarbot wintered at Port Royal in 1606–07 with the Mi'kmaq chief Membertou and the Order of Good Cheer; the Habitation at Quebec lost twenty of twenty-eight men in 1608–09. Crist and Sorg's 2014 paper on Burial 10 confirmed Champlain's autopsy. James Lind ran the citrus trial in 1747; Gilbert Blane's Royal Navy mandate followed in 1795.

🎵 Music: Original soundtrack created for this documentary

Sources
—————

Archives & Official Records
- Saint Croix Island International Historic Site (US National Park Service, with Parks Canada, 1984).
- Port-Royal National Historic Site (Parks Canada, Annapolis Royal, Nova Scotia).
- Bourgault and Fontaine memorial (2003) at Pointe-aux-Alouettes, Baie-Sainte-Catherine, Quebec.

Published Testimony & Primary Documents
- Samuel de Champlain — Les Voyages du Sieur de Champlain Xaintongeois (Paris, 1613); modern edition H. P. Biggar, The Works of Samuel de Champlain (Champlain Society, 1922–36).
- Samuel de Champlain — Des Sauvages (Paris, 1603).
- Jacques Cartier — Bref Recit (Paris, 1545); English translation in Hakluyt, The Principal Navigations (London, 1600).
- Marc Lescarbot — Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (Paris, 1609); modern translation W. L. Grant (Champlain Society, 1907–14).
- James Lind — A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753).

Books
- John Joseph Heagerty — Four Centuries of Medical History in Canada (Macmillan, 1928; reissued 1990).
- David Hackett Fischer — Champlain's Dream (Simon and Schuster, 2008).
- Clive M. Senior — A Nation of Pirates (David and Charles, 1976).
- Jacques Mathieu — L'Annedda: L'Arbre de Vie (Septentrion, 2009).
- Bruce G. Trigger — The Children of Aataentsic (McGill-Queen's University Press, 1976).
- Olive Patricia Dickason — Canada's First Nations (McClelland and Stewart, 1992).

Forensic / Scientific
- Thomas A. J. Crist and Marcella H. Sorg — "Adult Scurvy in New France: Samuel de Champlain's 'Mal de la Terre' at Saint Croix Island, 1604–1605," International Journal of Paleopathology 5 (2014): 95–105. Paleopathological diagnosis and identification of Burial 10's calvarial autopsy cut — the earliest physical evidence of a European autopsy in North America.
- Jacob W. Gruber — National Park Service field reports, 1968–69 excavation seasons, Saint Croix Island. Twenty-three sets of remains recovered.

Cross-verification
- Dictionary of Canadian Biography Online (biographi.ca) — entries on Champlain, Cartier, Dugua de Mons, Gravé Du Pont, Lescarbot, Poutrincourt, Membertou, Donnacona, Chauvin de Tonnetuit, Duval.
- The James Lind Library (jameslindlibrary.org), Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh.
- Encyclopedia Canadiana, Canadian Encyclopedia, and Encyclopædia Britannica.

Accuracy Notes
- The identity of "annedda" is not settled. Three serious candidates: Thuja occidentalis (eastern white cedar), Abies balsamea (balsam fir, Mathieu 2009), and Pinus strobus (white pine). The video uses eastern white cedar or hemlock as the most-cited possibilities. All three contain enough vitamin C to produce the cure.
- Champlain's birth year is contested between c. 1567 and c. 1574, giving an age range of 36 to 43 at his 1610 marriage and 61 to 68 at his 1635 death. The video presents both ranges.
- Membertou's claim of having been a grown man at Cartier's 1534 arrival — over 100 in 1607 — is presented by Lescarbot. Modern scholarship is skeptical of the literal centenarian reading.
- The "between seventy and eighty Frenchmen in four winters" aggregate sums: Saint Croix 1604–05 (35 of 79), Port Royal 1605–06 (~12 of ~45), Port Royal 1606–07 (~7 of ~70), Quebec 1608–09 (20 of 28). Port Royal figures approximate (Heagerty 1990); Saint Croix and Quebec exact (Champlain).
- The Quebec 1608–09 partition (seven of scurvy, thirteen of dysentery) is Champlain's own attribution. Some sources collapse it to scurvy alone; the video preserves Champlain's two-disease reading.
- The 211-year and 259-year arithmetic between Domagaya's 1536 cure and Lind's 1747 trial / Blane's 1795 mandate is calendar-exact. Some popular accounts give different figures because they date the cure to Cartier's 1545 publication rather than Domagaya's 1536 teaching.
- No authentic portrait of Champlain survives. The image on Canadian postage and textbooks is a nineteenth-century Ducornet lithograph (c. 1854) based on a Moncornet engraving of the French finance minister Michel Particelli d'Émery. The mistake is not seriously contested.
- Attribution of the bioarchaeology to Champlain's autopsies is the Crist and Sorg 2014 reading. Burial 10's name is not known; the burials are not individually identifiable beyond cemetery context.

snippet.title: Biggest 'Hold My Beer' Moments in History
snippet.description:
Biggest 'Hold My Beer' Moments in History
History is full of brilliant minds, careful planners, and legendary leaders. But sometimes, the people who change the story are the ones who look at common sense and politely throw it out the window.
In this video, we explore some of the biggest “Hold My Beer” moments in history — real events where people took unbelievable risks, made outrageous decisions, or somehow turned terrible ideas into unforgettable stories. From Lawnchair Larry flying over California in a chair tied to weather balloons, to Hannibal dragging elephants across the Alps, to Pepsi briefly ending up with Soviet ships, these are the historical moments that sound fake but actually happened.
This video was made by hand after careful research, detailed historical review, and fact-checking. Our goal is to make history educational without making it feel like homework. Every story is presented with context, humor, and clear explanations so you understand not only what happened, but why it mattered.
You’ll learn about strange military decisions, reckless leaders, impossible survival stories, ridiculous political moves, and people whose confidence levels were dangerously higher than their planning skills.
If you enjoy weird history, unbelievable true stories, dumb decisions that somehow worked, and historical facts that make you say “how was this real?”, this one is for you.
Like, subscribe, and tell us in the comments: who had the most outrageous “Hold My Beer” moment in history?

snippet.title: Weirdest Funerals In History That You Didn't Hear About
snippet.description:
Weirdest Funerals In History That You Didn't Hear About
Exploding kings, swearing parrots, stolen corpses, moon burials, motorcycle tombs, and one inventor buried inside a Pringles can. History has produced some truly unbelievable funerals, and these 33 strange burial stories prove that even death can become ridiculous.
In this episode of Blundera, we explore the weirdest funerals in history that sound fake but actually happened, or became famous through some of the wildest legends ever attached to real people. From William the Conqueror’s disastrous burial to Andrew Jackson’s foul-mouthed parrot, from Jeremy Bentham’s preserved body to Hunter S. Thompson’s cannon funeral, this is history at its most strange, darkly funny, and completely unhinged.
Expect strange historical facts, weird funeral customs, famous last sendoffs, bizarre burials, and the kind of stories your history teacher absolutely did not have time to explain.
Which funeral was the most insane? And which bizarre burial did we miss?
Subscribe to Blundera for more weird history, dumb mistakes, strange rituals, and unbelievable facts from the past.
